lessons.title: Atoms, Elements, Compounds and the Model of the Atom
lessons.description: Covers what are atoms?, elements and the periodic table, compounds and chemical formulas and more.
lessons.content_html:
What are Atoms?

Everything around us is made up of tiny particles called atoms. Atoms are incredibly small — about 0.1 nanometres across. To put this in perspective, if an atom was the size of a football, a football would be the size of Earth!

Key Fact

All substances are made of atoms. Atoms cannot be created or destroyed in chemical reactions.

Atoms are made up of three types of particles: protons, neutrons, and electrons. Understanding how these particles are arranged helps us understand how different elements behave and react with each other.

Elements and the Periodic Table

An element is a pure substance that contains only one type of atom. For example, oxygen contains only oxygen atoms, and carbon contains only carbon atoms. There are about 100 different elements, and they’re all organised in the periodic table.

Each element has a unique atomic number. This tells us how many protons are in each atom of that element. Hydrogen has atomic number 1 (1 proton), helium has atomic number 2 (2 protons), and so on.

Elements in the same column (group) of the periodic table have similar properties because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell. This affects how they react with other elements.

Compounds and Chemical Formulas

When atoms of different elements join together, they form compounds. For example, water (\(H_2O\)) is a compound made from hydrogen and oxygen atoms. The chemical formula tells us exactly which atoms are present and in what ratio.

Key Fact

In chemical formulas, the small numbers (subscripts) tell us how many atoms of each element are present. \(H_2O\) means 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom.

Common compounds you should know include:

  • Water: \(H_2O\) (hydrogen and oxygen)
  • Carbon dioxide: \(CO_2\) (carbon and oxygen)
  • Sodium chloride: \(NaCl\) (sodium and chlorine)
  • Methane: \(CH_4\) (carbon and hydrogen)

The Structure of the Atom

Modern atomic theory tells us that atoms have a specific structure. At the centre is the nucleus, which contains protons and neutrons. Around the nucleus, electrons move in regions called electron shells or energy levels.

Protons: Positively charged particles in the nucleus. The number of protons determines what element the atom is.

Neutrons: Neutral particles (no charge) in the nucleus. They add mass to the atom but don’t affect its chemical properties.

Electrons: Negatively charged particles that move around the nucleus in shells. They’re involved in chemical bonding.

The relative masses are important to remember: protons and neutrons each have a relative mass of 1, while electrons have a relative mass of almost zero (1/1836 to be precise).

How the Atomic Model Developed

Our understanding of atomic structure has changed dramatically over time as scientists gathered new evidence. This shows how scientific knowledge develops through experimentation and discovery.

1803

Dalton’s Atomic Theory

John Dalton proposed that all matter was made of tiny, indivisible particles called atoms. He thought atoms were like tiny solid spheres.

1897

Discovery of the Electron

J.J. Thomson discovered electrons and proposed the ‘plum pudding’ model — atoms were positive spheres with negative electrons embedded in them.

1909

Rutherford’s Gold Foil Experiment

Ernest Rutherford fired alpha particles at gold foil. Most passed through, but some bounced back, proving atoms have a tiny, dense nucleus.

1913

Bohr’s Model

Niels Bohr proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus in specific energy levels or shells, like planets around the sun.

Each new discovery built on previous work and led to a better understanding of atomic structure. This is a great example of how scientific knowledge is provisional — it can change when new evidence is discovered.

Mass Number and Atomic Number

Every element can be described using two important numbers. The atomic number tells us how many protons are in the nucleus. The mass number tells us the total number of protons and neutrons.

We can use these numbers to work out the number of each type of particle in an atom:

  • Number of protons = atomic number
  • Number of neutrons = mass number - atomic number
  • Number of electrons = number of protons (in a neutral atom)
Key Fact

In a neutral atom, the number of protons always equals the number of electrons. This means the positive and negative charges balance out.

Key Takeaways

  • All matter is made of atoms, which contain protons, neutrons, and electrons arranged with a nucleus at the centre
  • Elements contain only one type of atom, while compounds contain atoms of different elements chemically bonded together
  • Our model of atomic structure has evolved over time as scientists made new discoveries and gathered evidence
lessons.exam_tip_html: When drawing atomic structure diagrams, remember that the nucleus is much smaller than shown in most diagrams — if drawn to scale, it would be invisible! Also, make sure you can calculate the number of neutrons by subtracting atomic number from mass number. This type of calculation appears frequently in exam questions.

lessons.title: The Periodic Table and Its Groups
lessons.description: How elements are arranged in the periodic table and the properties of Groups 1, 7 and 0.
lessons.content_html:
The Development of the Periodic Table

Before the discovery of protons and neutrons, scientists attempted to classify elements by arranging them in order of atomic weight. Dmitri Mendeleev (1869) arranged elements in order of atomic weight but left gaps for undiscovered elements and swapped some elements so that those with similar properties lined up in the same columns. When elements such as gallium and germanium were later discovered and matched his predictions, his table was widely accepted.

The modern periodic table arranges elements in order of atomic number (not atomic weight). Elements in the same group (column) have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, giving them similar chemical properties. Elements in the same period (row) have the same number of electron shells.

Key Fact

Elements are arranged by atomic number. Groups (columns) share the same number of outer electrons and similar properties. Periods (rows) share the same number of electron shells. Metals are on the left; non-metals are on the right.

Group 1 — Alkali Metals

The alkali metals (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr) all have one electron in their outer shell. They are soft, have low density and react vigorously with water, producing a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas:

$$2Na + 2H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + H_2$$

Going down Group 1, reactivity increases because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and is more easily lost (less electrostatic attraction). The elements also have lower melting points and higher densities going down the group.

Group 7 — Halogens

The halogens (F, Cl, Br, I, At) have seven electrons in their outer shell. They exist as diatomic molecules (\(Cl_2\), \(Br_2\), etc.) and react with metals to form ionic compounds called halides (e.g. NaCl).

Going down Group 7, reactivity decreases because the outer shell is further from the nucleus, making it harder to gain an extra electron. A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from its compound, e.g. chlorine displaces bromine from potassium bromide.

Key Fact

Group 1: reactivity increases down the group (easier to lose outer electron). Group 7: reactivity decreases down the group (harder to gain an electron). These trends are opposite because metals lose electrons while non-metals gain them.

The noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn) have full outer electron shells, making them very stable and unreactive. They are used where inert gases are needed: helium in balloons and airships, neon in advertising signs, argon in light bulbs and welding. Boiling point increases down the group.

Transition metals are found in the central block of the periodic table. They have typical metallic properties: high melting points, high density, good conductors. Unlike Group 1 metals, transition metals are less reactive, harder and denser. They form coloured compounds and can act as catalysts (e.g. iron in the Haber process).
lessons.exam_tip_html: For Group 1: more shells = outer electron further from nucleus = weaker attraction = easier to lose = more reactive. For Group 7: more shells = outer shell further from nucleus = weaker attraction for incoming electron = harder to gain = less reactive.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The periodic table is arranged by atomic number; groups share outer electron count and similar properties.
  • Group 1 (alkali metals): reactivity increases down the group. Group 7 (halogens): reactivity decreases down the group.
  • Group 0 (noble gases) are unreactive because they have full outer electron shells.

lessons.title: Ionic, Covalent and Metallic Bonding
lessons.description: How atoms bond by transferring or sharing electrons, and the properties of metallic bonds.
lessons.content_html:
Ionic Bonding

When metals react with non-metals, electrons are transferred from the metal atom to the non-metal atom. The metal atom loses electrons to form a positive ion (cation), and the non-metal atom gains electrons to form a negative ion (anion). Both ions then have full outer electron shells and are stable.

The strong electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions is called an ionic bond. For example, in sodium chloride (NaCl), sodium loses one electron to become \(Na^+\) and chlorine gains one electron to become \(Cl^-\).

Key Fact

Ionic bonding: metal atoms lose electrons (form positive ions) and non-metal atoms gain electrons (form negative ions). The ions are held together by strong electrostatic attraction in a giant ionic lattice.

Covalent Bonding

When non-metals bond with other non-metals, they share pairs of electrons. This is called a covalent bond. Each shared pair of electrons counts as one bond. Examples include:

  • \(H_2\) — a single covalent bond (one shared pair).
  • \(O_2\) — a double covalent bond (two shared pairs: \(O=O\)).
  • \(N_2\) — a triple covalent bond (three shared pairs: \(N \equiv N\)).
  • \(H_2O\) — two single covalent bonds.
  • \(CH_4\) — four single covalent bonds.

You need to draw dot-and-cross diagrams showing how electrons are shared or transferred. For ionic bonding, show the transfer of electrons and the charges on the resulting ions. For covalent bonding, show the shared pairs of electrons in the overlap between atoms. Only show outer shell electrons. Use dots for one atom and crosses for the other.

Metallic Bonding

In metals, the outer electrons are delocalised — they leave their atoms and form a “sea” of electrons that can move freely through the structure. The metallic bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between the positive metal ions and this sea of delocalised electrons.

Key Fact

Metallic bonding: positive metal ions surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons. This explains why metals conduct electricity (delocalised electrons carry charge) and are malleable (layers of ions can slide over each other).

Ionic: transfer of electrons, metal + non-metal, forms a giant ionic lattice. Covalent: sharing of electrons, non-metal + non-metal, forms simple molecules or giant covalent structures. Metallic: delocalised electrons, metal atoms, forms a giant metallic structure.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the exam, you may be asked to draw dot-and-cross diagrams for ionic or covalent compounds. For ionic compounds, always show the electron transfer and write the charges (e.g. \(Na^+\), \(Cl^-\)). For covalent compounds, show the shared pairs in the overlap. Remember: ionic = transfer, covalent = sharing.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ionic bonding: electrons transferred from metal to non-metal, forming oppositely charged ions held in a lattice.
  • Covalent bonding: electrons shared between non-metal atoms to form molecules.
  • Metallic bonding: positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, explaining conductivity and malleability.

lessons.title: Structure, Properties and Carbon Allotropes
lessons.description: Giant ionic lattices, simple molecules, giant covalent structures, and allotropes of carbon.
lessons.content_html:
Properties of Ionic Compounds

Ionic compounds form giant ionic lattices — a regular arrangement of alternating positive and negative ions. The strong electrostatic forces between the ions act in all directions, giving ionic compounds these properties:

  • High melting and boiling points — a lot of energy is needed to overcome the strong ionic bonds.
  • Conduct electricity when molten or dissolved — the ions are free to move and carry charge. They do not conduct when solid because the ions are fixed in position.
Key Fact

Ionic compounds: high melting points (strong bonds in all directions), conduct when molten or dissolved (ions free to move), do not conduct when solid (ions fixed in lattice).

Properties of Simple Molecular Substances

Simple molecules (e.g. \(H_2O\), \(CO_2\), \(O_2\)) have strong covalent bonds within the molecule but weak intermolecular forces between molecules. This gives them:

  • Low melting and boiling points — little energy is needed to overcome the weak intermolecular forces (not the covalent bonds).
  • Do not conduct electricity — no free electrons or ions to carry charge.

As molecules get larger, the intermolecular forces become stronger, so larger molecules tend to have higher boiling points.

Giant Covalent Structures

Giant covalent structures have millions of atoms connected by covalent bonds in a continuous network. They have very high melting points because many strong covalent bonds must be broken. Examples include diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide.

Diamond: each carbon atom bonds to four others in a rigid tetrahedral structure. Very hard, high melting point, does not conduct electricity (no free electrons or ions).

Graphite: each carbon bonds to three others, forming flat layers with weak forces between them. The fourth electron is delocalised, allowing graphite to conduct electricity. Layers can slide over each other, making it soft and slippery (useful as a lubricant).

Graphene: a single layer of graphite — one atom thick. It is very strong, light, and an excellent conductor of electricity and heat. Fullerenes (e.g. \(C_{60}\) buckminsterfullerene) are carbon molecules shaped like hollow spheres or tubes. Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes with remarkable strength and conductivity.

Key Fact

Diamond: 4 bonds per carbon, very hard, doesn’t conduct. Graphite: 3 bonds per carbon + delocalised electrons, conducts electricity, layers slide. Graphene: single layer of graphite, strongest known material, conducts.

Polymers are very large molecules made up of many repeating units called monomers. They have relatively strong intermolecular forces between the long chains, so they tend to be solid at room temperature. Examples include poly(ethene) and poly(propene).
lessons.exam_tip_html: When explaining properties, always link structure to property. For example: “Graphite conducts electricity because each carbon atom only forms three covalent bonds, leaving one delocalised electron per atom that is free to move and carry charge.” Don’t just state the property — explain WHY using the bonding model.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ionic compounds: giant lattice, high melting point, conduct when molten/dissolved.
  • Simple molecules: weak intermolecular forces, low melting point, don’t conduct.
  • Giant covalent: very high melting point. Diamond (hard, insulator), graphite (conducts, layers slide), graphene (single layer, strongest material).

lessons.title: Quantitative Chemistry: Mass, Moles and Concentrations
lessons.description: Covers what are moles?, calculating moles from mass, concentration of solutions and more.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Moles?

A mole is the unit chemists use to count atoms, molecules and ions. Just like a dozen equals 12 items, one mole equals 6.02 × 10²³ particles. This huge number is called Avogadro's constant.

Key Fact

One mole of any element has a mass in grams equal to its relative atomic mass. For example, one mole of carbon (relative atomic mass 12) has a mass of 12g.

The molar mass connects the microscopic world of atoms to the macroscopic world we can measure. For compounds, we add up the relative atomic masses of all atoms present.

Calculating Moles from Mass

The fundamental equation linking moles, mass and molar mass is:

\(\text{number of moles} = \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{molar mass}}\)

This can be rearranged to find mass or molar mass depending on what information you're given.

Calculate the number of moles in 44g of carbon dioxide (CO₂).

Step 1: Find the molar mass of CO₂

Carbon: 1 × 12 = 12g/mol

Oxygen: 2 × 16 = 32g/mol

Total molar mass = 12 + 32 = 44g/mol

Step 2: Apply the formula

\(\text{moles} = \frac{44}{44} = 1 \text{ mole}\)

Concentration of Solutions

When substances dissolve in water, we create solutions. The concentration tells us how much solute is dissolved in a given volume of solution.

Key Fact

Concentration can be measured in g/dm³ (mass concentration) or mol/dm³ (molar concentration). Both are essential for different types of calculations.

The two main concentration equations you need to know are:

$$\text{concentration (g/dm³)} = \frac{\text{mass of solute (g)}}{\text{volume of solution (dm³)}}$$

\(\text{concentration (mol/dm³)} = \frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{volume of solution (dm³)}}\)

Remember these volume conversions:

  • 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³ = 1000 ml = 1 litre
  • To convert cm³ to dm³: divide by 1000
  • To convert dm³ to cm³: multiply by 1000

Calculating Masses in Reactions

Chemical equations show the molar ratios between reactants and products. We can use these ratios along with molar masses to calculate the masses of substances involved in reactions.

The process follows these steps:

  1. Write the balanced chemical equation
  2. Identify the molar ratio from the equation
  3. Calculate moles of the known substance
  4. Use the molar ratio to find moles of unknown substance
  5. Convert moles back to mass using molar mass

Calculate the mass of water produced when 16g of methane burns completely.

\(CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O\)

Step 1: Calculate moles of methane

Molar mass of CH₄ = 12 + (4 × 1) = 16 g/mol

\(\text{moles of CH}_4 = \frac{16}{16} = 1 \text{ mole}\)

Step 2: Use molar ratio

From equation: 1 mole CH₄ produces 2 moles H₂O

Therefore: moles of H₂O = 1 × 2 = 2 moles

Step 3: Convert to mass

Molar mass of H₂O = (2 × 1) + 16 = 18 g/mol

\(\text{mass of H}_2\text{O} = 2 × 18 = 36\text{g}\)

Limiting Reactants

In many reactions, one reactant runs out before the others. This limiting reactant determines how much product can be formed.

To identify the limiting reactant, calculate how many moles of each reactant you have, then compare this to the molar ratios in the balanced equation. The reactant that would be used up first is the limiting reactant.

Common Calculation Mistakes

Students often make errors when working with quantitative chemistry. Always check your balanced equations are correct before starting calculations. Make sure you convert units properly — especially converting cm³ to dm³ for concentration calculations. Remember that molar mass uses the relative atomic mass from the periodic table, and for compounds you must add up all the atoms present.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In moles calculations, always show your working clearly. Start by writing the equation you're using, substitute the numbers, then calculate the answer. Check your units match throughout — if concentration is in mol/dm³, make sure volume is in dm³ not cm³. For mass calculation questions, always write the balanced equation first as this shows the examiner you understand the molar ratios.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • One mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles and has a mass equal to the relative formula mass in grams
  • Use moles = mass ÷ molar mass to convert between mass and moles
  • Concentration links the amount of solute to the volume of solution using mass/volume or moles/volume

lessons.title: Reactivity of Metals and Metal Extraction
lessons.description: The reactivity series, displacement reactions, and how metals are extracted from their ores.
lessons.content_html:
The Reactivity Series

Metals can be arranged in order of their reactivity — this is called the reactivity series. The most reactive metals (potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium) react vigorously with water and acids. Less reactive metals (zinc, iron, copper, silver, gold) react more slowly or not at all.

A more reactive metal will displace a less reactive metal from its compound. For example, if iron is placed in copper sulfate solution, the iron displaces the copper:

$$Fe + CuSO_4 \rightarrow FeSO_4 + Cu$$

Key Fact

The reactivity series (most to least reactive): K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, C, Zn, Fe, H, Cu, Ag, Au. Carbon and hydrogen are included as reference points. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound.

Extraction of Metals

Metals are found in the Earth’s crust, often combined with other elements in ores. The method of extraction depends on the metal’s position in the reactivity series:

  • Metals less reactive than carbon (e.g. iron, copper, zinc) are extracted by reduction with carbon. Carbon is cheaper and more reactive, so it removes the oxygen from the metal oxide.
  • Metals more reactive than carbon (e.g. aluminium, sodium, potassium) must be extracted by electrolysis, which is more expensive because it requires large amounts of electricity.

For example, iron is extracted from iron oxide using carbon in a blast furnace:

$$2Fe_2O_3 + 3C \rightarrow 4Fe + 3CO_2$$

Oxidation is the gain of oxygen (or loss of electrons). Reduction is the loss of oxygen (or gain of electrons). Remember: OIL RIG — Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain. In a displacement reaction, the more reactive metal is oxidised (loses electrons) and the less reactive metal ion is reduced (gains electrons).

Key Fact

Metals below carbon in the reactivity series are extracted by reduction with carbon. Metals above carbon need electrolysis. Oxidation = gain of oxygen / loss of electrons. Reduction = loss of oxygen / gain of electrons.

Recycling metals saves energy (less needed than extraction from ore), reduces the use of limited ore resources, reduces waste going to landfill, and reduces environmental damage from mining and carbon emissions. However, collection and sorting can be difficult, and recycled metals may be impure.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing equations for displacement reactions, always check your reactivity series first. The more reactive metal replaces the less reactive one. For extraction questions, state whether the metal is above or below carbon and therefore whether it needs electrolysis or reduction with carbon.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The reactivity series ranks metals from most to least reactive; more reactive metals displace less reactive ones.
  • Metals below carbon are extracted by reduction with carbon; metals above carbon need electrolysis.
  • OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons, Reduction Is Gain. Recycling metals saves energy and resources.

lessons.title: Reactions of Acids, pH and Neutralisation
lessons.description: Acid-base reactions, the pH scale, neutralisation, and making salts from acids.
lessons.content_html:
Acids, Bases and the pH Scale

An acid is a substance that produces hydrogen ions (\(H^+\)) when dissolved in water. A base is a substance that can neutralise an acid. An alkali is a soluble base that produces hydroxide ions (\(OH^-\)) in water.

The pH scale runs from 0 to 14. Acids have a pH below 7, neutral solutions have a pH of 7, and alkalis have a pH above 7. pH can be measured with universal indicator or a pH probe.

Key Fact

Acids produce \(H^+\) ions in water; alkalis produce \(OH^-\) ions. The pH scale: 0–6 = acidic, 7 = neutral, 8–14 = alkaline. Neutralisation: \(H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O\).

Neutralisation Reactions

Neutralisation occurs when an acid reacts with a base. The ionic equation is:

$$H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O$$

The key reactions of acids are:

  • Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen. E.g. \(Mg + 2HCl \rightarrow MgCl_2 + H_2\)
  • Acid + metal oxide → salt + water. E.g. \(CuO + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow CuSO_4 + H_2O\)
  • Acid + metal hydroxide → salt + water. E.g. \(NaOH + HCl \rightarrow NaCl + H_2O\)
  • Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. E.g. \(CaCO_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_2 + H_2O + CO_2\)

The salt produced depends on which acid is used: hydrochloric acid (\(HCl\)) makes chlorides, sulfuric acid (\(H_2SO_4\)) makes sulfates, and nitric acid (\(HNO_3\)) makes nitrates.

To make a pure, dry salt: add an excess of insoluble base or metal oxide to the acid, filter off the excess solid, then evaporate the water from the filtrate to leave salt crystals. This is Required Practical 1.

Key Fact

HCl → chlorides. \(H_2SO_4\) → sulfates. \(HNO_3\) → nitrates. To predict the salt name: metal name + acid type (e.g. magnesium + sulfuric acid = magnesium sulfate).

Strong acids (e.g. hydrochloric, sulfuric, nitric acid) fully ionise in water — every acid molecule releases its \(H^+\) ions. Weak acids (e.g. ethanoic acid, citric acid) only partially ionise — an equilibrium is established between ionised and un-ionised molecules. At the same concentration, a strong acid has a lower pH than a weak acid.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When predicting the products of an acid reaction, identify the acid (for the salt type) and the base (for the metal in the salt). Then write: salt + water (for bases/oxides/hydroxides) or salt + water + CO\(_2\) (for carbonates). Always balance your equations.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Acids produce \(H^+\) ions, alkalis produce \(OH^-\) ions. Neutralisation: \(H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O\).
  • Acid + base → salt + water. HCl gives chlorides, \(H_2SO_4\) gives sulfates, \(HNO_3\) gives nitrates.
  • Strong acids fully ionise; weak acids partially ionise. A strong acid at the same concentration has a lower pH than a weak acid.

lessons.title: Electrolysis
lessons.description: How electrolysis breaks down ionic compounds using electricity, including aluminium extraction.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Electrolysis?

Electrolysis is the process of using electricity to break down an ionic compound into its elements. The compound being broken down is called the electrolyte and must be either molten or dissolved in water so that the ions are free to move.

The electrolyte is placed between two electrodes: the cathode (negative electrode) attracts positive metal ions, and the anode (positive electrode) attracts negative non-metal ions.

Key Fact

Electrolysis: positive ions (cations) move to the cathode (negative electrode), negative ions (anions) move to the anode (positive electrode). At the cathode, metals are deposited. At the anode, non-metals are released.

At the cathode, positive metal ions gain electrons (reduction) to form metal atoms. At the anode, negative ions lose electrons (oxidation) to form atoms or molecules. Remember: PANIC — Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode.

Electrolysis of Molten Compounds

When a molten binary ionic compound (e.g. lead bromide, \(PbBr_2\)) is electrolysed:

  • Cathode: \(Pb^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Pb\) (lead metal is deposited — reduction).
  • Anode: \(2Br^- \rightarrow Br_2 + 2e^-\) (bromine gas is released — oxidation).

When an ionic compound is dissolved in water, there are additional \(H^+\) and \(OH^-\) ions from the water. The rules for predicting products at each electrode are:

Cathode: If the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, hydrogen gas is produced. If less reactive than hydrogen, the metal is deposited.

Anode: If a halide ion is present, the halogen is produced. If no halide is present, oxygen is produced (from \(OH^-\) ions).

Extraction of Aluminium

Aluminium is too reactive to be extracted by reduction with carbon, so it is extracted by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide (\(Al_2O_3\)). The aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite to lower the melting point and reduce energy costs.

At the cathode: \(Al^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow Al\) (aluminium is deposited).

At the anode: \(2O^{2-} \rightarrow O_2 + 4e^-\) (oxygen is released). The carbon anodes gradually burn away because the oxygen reacts with them at high temperature, so they need regular replacement.

Key Fact

Aluminium extraction: electrolysis of \(Al_2O_3\) dissolved in cryolite. Al deposited at cathode, \(O_2\) at anode. Carbon anodes burn away and need replacing. The process uses large amounts of electricity, making it expensive.

Required Practical 4 involves electrolysing aqueous solutions using inert (carbon or platinum) electrodes. You observe the products at each electrode and test them: hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop, chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper, and oxygen relights a glowing splint.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Always state which electrode each product forms at and whether the process at that electrode is oxidation or reduction. Remember PANIC (Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode) and OIL RIG. For aqueous solutions, you must apply the rules for competing ions (metal vs hydrogen at cathode, halide vs hydroxide at anode).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Electrolysis uses electricity to decompose ionic compounds; the electrolyte must be molten or dissolved.
  • Cathode (negative): metal deposited or hydrogen released (reduction). Anode (positive): non-metal released (oxidation).
  • Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis of \(Al_2O_3\) in cryolite. Carbon anodes burn away and need replacing.

lessons.title: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions
lessons.description: Covers introduction to energy changes, exothermic reactions, endothermic reactions and more.
lessons.content_html:
Introduction to Energy Changes

All chemical reactions involve energy changes. When chemical bonds are broken and new bonds are formed, energy is either released to the surroundings or absorbed from the surroundings. Understanding these energy changes is crucial for predicting how reactions behave and their practical applications.

Key Fact

Energy is required to break chemical bonds and energy is released when new bonds are formed.

Exothermic Reactions

An exothermic reaction is one where energy is released to the surroundings. In these reactions, more energy is released when new bonds form than is needed to break the original bonds. This results in a net release of energy, usually observed as an increase in temperature of the surroundings.

Common exothermic reactions include combustion reactions, such as burning methane: \(CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O\). Other examples include neutralisation reactions between acids and bases, and many oxidation reactions.

Hand warmers used in winter often contain iron powder that undergoes an exothermic oxidation reaction with oxygen from the air, releasing heat energy.

Endothermic Reactions

An endothermic reaction is one where energy is absorbed from the surroundings. In these reactions, more energy is needed to break the original bonds than is released when new bonds form. This results in a net absorption of energy, usually observed as a decrease in temperature of the surroundings.

Key Fact

In endothermic reactions, the temperature of the surroundings decreases because energy is absorbed from them.

Thermal decomposition reactions are typically endothermic. For example, heating copper carbonate: \(CuCO_3 \rightarrow CuO + CO_2\). The reaction requires continuous heating to proceed.

Sports injury packs often contain ammonium nitrate that dissolves endothermically in water, absorbing heat and cooling the injured area.

Energy Profiles and Activation Energy

Energy profile diagrams show how the energy of reactants and products changes during a chemical reaction. These diagrams help us understand the energy requirements and energy changes involved in chemical processes.

The activation energy is the minimum energy required for reactants to overcome the energy barrier and start reacting. Even exothermic reactions require this initial energy input to break the first bonds and get the reaction started.

Key Fact

All reactions, whether exothermic or endothermic, require activation energy to begin.

Bond Breaking and Bond Making

During chemical reactions, existing bonds in reactant molecules must be broken before new bonds can form in the product molecules. Bond breaking is always an endothermic process — it requires energy input. Bond making is always an exothermic process — it releases energy.

The overall energy change of a reaction depends on the balance between energy required for bond breaking and energy released during bond making. If more energy is released than absorbed, the reaction is exothermic. If more energy is absorbed than released, the reaction is endothermic.

The energy change of a reaction can be calculated using bond energies:

\(\text{Energy change} = \text{Energy required to break bonds} - \text{Energy released making bonds}\)

If the result is positive, the reaction is endothermic. If negative, the reaction is exothermic.

Practical Applications

Understanding energy changes in chemical reactions has many practical applications. Exothermic reactions are used in heating systems, self-heating food containers, and rocket fuels. Endothermic reactions are used in instant cold packs for sports injuries and in some industrial processes where cooling is required.

In everyday life, we rely on the exothermic combustion of fuels for heating our homes and powering vehicles. The energy released during these reactions provides the thermal energy we need for warmth and the kinetic energy for movement.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When identifying whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic, look for temperature changes mentioned in the question. Remember that exothermic reactions release heat (temperature increases), while endothermic reactions absorb heat (temperature decreases). For energy profile diagrams, check whether products are at a higher or lower energy level than reactants.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings, causing temperature to increase
  • Endothermic reactions absorb energy from the surroundings, causing temperature to decrease
  • All reactions require activation energy to overcome the initial energy barrier
  • The overall energy change depends on the balance between bond breaking (endothermic) and bond making (exothermic)

practice_questions.text: Calculate the energy change for the reaction: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. Bond energies: H-H = 436 kJ/mol, Cl-Cl = 243 kJ/mol, H-Cl = 432 kJ/mol. State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Energy required to break bonds = 436 + 243 = 679 kJ/mol. 1 mark: Energy released making bonds = 2 × 432 = 864 kJ/mol. 1 mark: Energy change = 679 - 864 = -185 kJ/mol. 1 mark: Correct calculation with units. 1 mark: The reaction is exothermic. 1 mark: Because energy change is negative/more energy is released than absorbed.

practice_questions.text: Draw and label an energy profile diagram for an endothermic reaction. Include reactants, products, activation energy, and overall energy change.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Reactants at lower energy level than products. 1 mark: Activation energy barrier shown as peak above reactants. 1 mark: All components correctly labelled (reactants, products, activation energy, overall energy change). 1 mark: Axes labelled (energy on y-axis, reaction pathway/time on x-axis).

practice_questions.text: Explain why bond breaking is endothermic and bond making is exothermic, using ideas about energy and forces between atoms.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Bond breaking is endothermic because energy is required/absorbed. 1 mark: Energy is needed to overcome the attractive forces between bonded atoms. 1 mark: Work must be done to separate the atoms against these attractive forces. 1 mark: Bond making is exothermic because energy is released. 1 mark: When atoms come together, attractive forces pull them closer. 1 mark: This releases energy as the atoms reach a more stable/lower energy state.
